subject: Re: Borderless Deployment Safeguards — network demarcation & scenario Qs
messages:
From: Jennifer Stone <jennifer.stone@asteria-health.com>
To: laura.bennett@redwoodinference.com
Cc: security@asteria-health.com
Date: 2027-06-20T09:15:00-07:00
Subject: Borderless deployment — request for topology, attack scenarios

Hi Laura,

Thanks for the quick intro on Friday. As we evaluate Redwood for a regulated deployment, Asteria’s security team has asked for a concise packet describing the network demarcation and realistic attack scenarios for what we’re calling a “borderless" (private control plane + customer-managed VPC) deployment. Specifically we need:

- A network/topology diagram showing control plane vs data plane separation, peering/egress boundaries, and tenant circuits.
- A short description of the isolation model (tenancy, subnets, sidecars, proxies).
- 3–5 prioritized threat scenarios (lateral movement, egress/exfiltration, KV cache poisoning, supply-chain/model compromise) and the mitigations you recommend.
- Any evidence artifacts you can point us to (flow logs, attestation steps, SOC2 sections, sample audit log export).

Target delivery: ideally by COB Thursday so our InfoSec can review before Friday’s risk meeting. If you have a one-page executive summary and a more technical appendix, that would be perfect.

Thanks — we’re excited to move this forward.

Jennifer Stone
Director, Security Engineering
Asteria Health

Hi Jennifer — thanks for the clear list. Attaching a concise packet that addresses each ask: a one-page executive summary plus a technical appendix and an updated topology diagram. I’ve included the high-level answers below and attached the artifacts.

Attachments:
- redwood-borderless-topology-v1.pdf (PDF schematic, annotated)
- network-diagram-v2.png (PNG: logical zones + egress paths)

Executive summary (short):
- Deployment model: Redwood provides a private control plane (customer-private control plane option) while the inference data plane runs inside the customer’s VPC or a dedicated Redwood VPC with strict tenant demarcation.
- Isolation primitives: per-tenant subnets, sidecar proxies for model runtime, per-instance kernel/process hardening, KV cache isolation (per-tenant keying), and hardware-backed key management (KMS/HSM).
- Egress & routing: explicit egress gateways (customer-managed or Redwood-managed), allowlist-based egress policies, optional NAT gateway, and flow logging for all egress paths.
- Threat posture: prioritized scenarios (lateral move from compromised compute, egress/exfil via sidecar, KV cache integrity attack, model-weight tampering) with measurable mitigations and audit trails.

Key design notes (technical):
- Control vs data plane: control plane signaling uses mutually authenticated channels; the control plane has no direct access to tenant data at rest (encrypted) or in KV caches (encrypted with tenant-bound keys).
- Sidecar architecture: each model runtime is fronted by a lightweight sidecar that enforces TLS, token auth, rate limits, and token-scoped cache access. Sidecars run in separate processes/containers with minimal privileges.
- Network fencing: CIDR scoping per-tenant, security groups with least-privilege rules, and segmentation enforced via routing + service mesh policies.
- Observability & evidence: VPC Flow Logs, application audit logs (token usage, model version rollouts), per-tenant request traces exportable to S3/GCS, and an evidence package we can produce for SOC2 timelines.

I’ve asked our Security PM and one of our runtime engineers to add an annotated threat scenarios doc and tighten some language around mitigations; they’ll follow with a short appendix and a more detailed attack-path matrix.

Let me know if you want the topology exported as a Terraform-friendly reference or a Visio/PNG.

Best,

Laura Bennett
Enterprise Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

Laura — draft below (I attached a structured doc). I kept it technical and prioritized attacker goals and mitigations. Feel free to trim.

Attachments: threat-scenarios-annotated.docx (contains scenario matrix and recommended evidence exports)

Scenario A — Lateral movement from a compromised compute instance- Attack path: tenant compute compromised (stolen API key or vulnerable container) => attempt to enumerate adjacent tenant subnets / probe sidecar endpoints => try to exfil KV cache or request data via model endpoints.
- Mitigations: strict per-tenant subnets + security groups; mTLS between runtime and sidecar; sidecar enforces token-scoped cache access; process/container isolation (seccomp + user namespaces); KV cache encryption with tenant-bound keys (KMS/HSM).
- Evidence: VPC Flow Logs showing blocked cross-tenant flows; audit log of token usage; host-level attestations (AMI/image-signature + boot-time measurements).

Scenario B — Egress/exfil via sidecar or misconfigured NAT- Attack path: an attacker uses a forged request or compromised credential to provoke large outbound requests to attacker-controlled host.
- Mitigations: egress allowlist at gateway, per-tenant rate limiting, request size limits, DNS egress filtering, optional forced-proxy for all outbound traffic, and flow-log alerting.
- Evidence: aggregated egress logs, alerting runbook screenshots, example allowlist config.

Scenario C — KV cache integrity / poisoning- Attack path: attempt to inject poisoned cache entries to affect model outputs or leak data across requests.
- Mitigations: cryptographic MACs on cache entries with tenant-scoped keys, per-token TTLs, validation on cache retrieval, and separate cache instances per-tenant where possible.
- Evidence: cache audit logs, cache hit/miss telemetry, per-tenant cache metrics export.

Scenario D — Supply chain / model-weight tampering- Attack path: compromise package manager or model store to push modified weights.
- Mitigations: signed model artifacts, image-reproducibility checks, controlled rollout with canary and automated QA/eval gates, offline signing (HSM) for production artifacts.
- Evidence: model-signature records, rollout audit trail, canary evaluation results.

Operational controls to call out:
- Network: VPC Flow Logs, AWS/GCP PrivateLink or VPC peering for data plane isolation, egress gateway with allowlist.
- Host/runtime: seccomp profiles, read-only root fs, kernel patch management, and limited syscall surfaces.
- Keys and secrets: per-tenant KMS keys, HSM-backed signing, short-lived tokens, and automated rotation.
- Observability: centralized audit exports, per-route latency/cost traces, and automated regression alerts on model outputs.

I added small implementation notes for sidecar design and a checklist for producing evidence exports.

— Karthik
